clue.text: Sound stone-fruit, but appears to sag

indicators.note: Sound at the head of the clue says the next word is to be taken as it is spoken

parts.note: a drupe is the botanical name for a stone fruit such as a plum or cherry

explanation.surface: A plum or cherry that looks limp and seems to be wilting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like an adjective meaning healthy, contradicting the sagging, but it signals a homophone of DRUPE.
explanation.definitionFit: To droop is to hang down limply, the same as sagging.

clue.text: Soft fruit could be said at first to vanish

indicators.note: at first places the rearranged word ahead of the remaining pieces
could be suggests the letters of the word said might be rearranged into something else

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical abbreviation for soft
a pear is a common fruit

explanation.surface: Soft fruit, one might say, is the first thing to disappear from the bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' looks like a verb of speaking but is anagram fodder; 'Soft' is the musical p for piano.
explanation.definitionFit: To disappear is to pass out of sight, which is what vanishing means.

clue.text: Love to be a green girl

parts.note: love is a score of nil in tennis, written as O
to live is to be, to exist

explanation.surface: Love transforms an inexperienced young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'green girl' reads as a naive young woman, but it covers two senses at once: a shade of green and a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Olive is both a dull yellowish-green colour and a traditional female first name.

clue.text: In Puerto Rico gun-girl is carried by a donkey

indicators.note: In before the island's name says the woman sits inside its abbreviation

parts.note: Annie is the sharpshooting heroine of the musical Annie Get Your Gun

explanation.surface: A woman with a gun in Puerto Rico rides on a donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition stands for 'something carried by a donkey'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pannier is a basket slung on each side of a pack animal for carrying loads.

clue.text: Such a career for Gilbert's Frederic, Slave of Duty

definitions.text: Such a career for Gilbert's Frederic, Slave of Duty

parts.words: Such a career for Gilbert's Frederic, Slave of Duty
parts.note: Frederic, hero of Gilbert and Sullivan's The Pirates of Penzance (subtitled The Slave of Duty), is apprenticed by mistake to a band of sea robbers

explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert and Sullivan were the Victorian authors of comic operas; Frederic's nurse misheard 'pilot' and bound him to buccaneers.
explanation.definitionFit: Piratical means belonging to sea robbers, the trade Frederic was bound to follow.

clue.text: What's yours? Could be just my meat

definitions.text: What's yours? Could be just my meat

parts.words: What's yours? Could be just my meat
parts.note: plays on the proverb that one man's meat is another man's toxin, and on the barroom question about what drink you will have

explanation.walkthrough: 'What's yours?' is a pub host's offer of a drink, and 'name your poison' is the stock reply's cue; 'my meat' completes the proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: A toxic substance is the opposite of nourishment in the proverb about meat for one being harmful to another.

clue.text: Some behaved so badly in Hamlet's stately home

definitions.text: Some behaved so badly in Hamlet's stately home

parts.words: Some behaved so badly in Hamlet's stately home
parts.note: echoes Marcellus's line that something is amiss in the state of Denmark, Hamlet's home

explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' is the start of 'something', and 'stately home' hides 'the state'; the line runs 'Something is rotten in the state of Denmark'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rottenly means in a corrupt or badly behaved manner, as in Shakespeare's famous line.

clue.text: Public official finds plant-disease in part of course

indicators.note: in says the plant disease is placed within the stretch of golf course

parts.note: a tee is the part of a golf course where each hole begins
rust is a fungal disease of plants

explanation.surface: An official discovers blight on a section of the golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: The Public Trustee is a British official who administers estates and trusts.
explanation.definitionFit: A trustee holds and manages property on behalf of others, a role filled officially by the Public Trustee.

clue.text: Pugnacious hairdresser upset Argentine lady

parts.note: a comb is a tool that dresses hair

indicators.note: upset in a down clue says the lady's name is turned upside down, read bottom to top

parts.note: Evita is Eva Perón, the Argentine first lady

explanation.surface: An aggressive hairdresser has annoyed a woman from Argentina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hairdresser' suggests a stylist but is a tool; 'upset' turns EVITA into ATIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Combative means eager to fight, which is what pugnacious means.

clue.text: British Isle has lovely borders and exotic interior

indicators.note: interior says the foreign word goes inside the edge letters
borders asks for only the edge letters of the word lovely

parts.note: und is German for and, so an exotic, foreign and

explanation.surface: A British island with beautiful edges and an unusual interior.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exotic' does not mean unusual here: it asks for a foreign word for 'and'. Lundy lies in the Bristol Channel.
explanation.definitionFit: Lundy is a small island in the Bristol Channel off the coast of Devon.

clue.text: Carlyle's political economist a dismal one?

definitions.text: Carlyle's political economist a dismal one?

parts.words: Carlyle's political economist a dismal one?
parts.note: Thomas Carlyle called economics the dismal science, so its practitioner would be a dismal practitioner of that science

explanation.walkthrough: Carlyle was a Victorian Scottish essayist whose phrase 'the dismal science' still describes economics.
explanation.definitionFit: An economist practises what Carlyle called a science, making him a researcher in that field.

clue.text: Demoralize member of international organization

parts.note: UN is the United Nations
a man is a member of a team or body

explanation.surface: To dishearten one of the delegates at the United Nations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'member' is a person here, a UN man, read as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To unman is to deprive someone of courage, to dishearten.

clue.text: One the state may perhaps appoint, entirely, authorized

indicators.note: perhaps hints the two words that follow may be rearranged into a different form

explanation.surface: Someone the state might appoint with complete authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' asks for APPOINT and ENTIRELY, fifteen letters, to be rearranged; the opening words describe such an envoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Plenipotentiary, as an adjective, means invested with full powers to act, so fully empowered.

clue.text: Politician in Ireland's old music-hall

indicators.note: in places the politician inside the name of the country

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for Ireland
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician in an Irish music hall of former days.
explanation.walkthrough: The Empire was a common name for British variety theatres, such as the Empire, Leicester Square.
explanation.definitionFit: The Empire was a famous London variety theatre, typical of the old halls where popular entertainment was staged.

clue.text: Group isn't involved in striking attitudes

indicators.note: involved suggests the letters of the two words are tangled together into a new order

explanation.surface: A group declines to take part in labour strikes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'striking' looks like industrial action alongside 'Group'; it means adopting poses.
explanation.definitionFit: Posturing is adopting affected poses, which is what striking attitudes describes.

clue.text: Play that won a speed record

explanation.surface: A stage drama that broke a speed record.
explanation.walkthrough: The Blue Bird is a play by Maurice Maeterlinck; Bluebird was the name of the Campbells' record-breaking cars and boats.
explanation.definitionFit: Maeterlinck's fairy play is The Blue Bird, and Malcolm and Donald Campbell set land and water speed records in vehicles called Bluebird.

clue.text: Profane violation of seed packing-case

indicators.note: violation of says the word seed is abused and so mixed up

parts.note: a crate is a wooden packing case

explanation.surface: Sacrilegious damage done to a seed box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Profane' is a verb here, matching the verb answer, though it reads at first as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To desecrate is to treat something sacred with violence or disrespect, to profane it.

clue.text: In no real sense this property is private

definitions.text: In no real sense this property

explanation.surface: This piece of property is in no real sense private.
explanation.walkthrough: In law, real property is land and buildings; movable goods are personal property, so 'no real' points to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Personal property is the legal term for goods as opposed to real estate, and personal also means private or individual.

clue.text: Was still besieging island that wouldn't surrender

indicators.note: besieging says the word for being still surrounds the island

parts.note: rested means remained still

explanation.surface: Kept quiet while blockading an island that refused to give in.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads as a past-tense verb: resisted means held out and wouldn't surrender.
explanation.definitionFit: To have resisted is to have held out against attack rather than yield.

clue.text: Sign of stinginess?

parts.note: reads as a mark of meanness, but stinginess is split as sting-iness: the zodiac sign of the creature with a sting

explanation.walkthrough: The zodiac sign is represented by a scorpion, famous for its sting.
explanation.definitionFit: Scorpio is the zodiac sign of the scorpion, an animal with a venomous sting.

clue.text: Sailor Queen in a convent?

parts.note: AB is an able-bodied seaman
Bess is the pet name of Queen Elizabeth I

explanation.surface: A naval monarch living in a nunnery.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example: the woman who reigns in a convent.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbess is the female superior of an abbey of nuns, its ruling head.

clue.text: Reserve A, we hear, is bunch of 21s

indicators.note: we hear says the preceding words are to be heard spoken

parts.note: to reserve is to book, followed by the letter A

explanation.surface: Seat A has been reserved, it is said, for a cluster of blooms.
explanation.walkthrough: The French word is pronounced boo-KAY, like 'book A'; 21s refers to the answer at 21 down, blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: A bouquet is an arranged bunch of blooms.

clue.text: River bed growth?

explanation.surface: Something growing in a riverbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River' here is something that flows, so a 'flow-er'; a garden bed's growth is a bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: A thing that flows is jokingly a river, and a bloom is what grows in a garden bed.

clue.text: Artist of no high standing

parts.note: reads as an obscure painter, but means one who literally stood very short, the French painter of Montmartre stunted by childhood fractures

explanation.walkthrough: 'no high standing' suggests low reputation; it is about physical height.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, the French painter of Paris nightlife, was famously short in stature.

clue.text: Like toothpaste coming out the wrong way

indicators.note: the wrong way says the word for a first appearance is read backwards

parts.note: a debut is a coming out, a first appearance in society

explanation.surface: Toothpaste squeezed out of its container in the wrong direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming out' pairs with toothpaste as squeezing, but it is a debutante's coming out, DEBUT, turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Toothpaste is sold in tubes, so it is packaged that way.

clue.text: See Colman act to music

parts.note: Ronald Colman was a British film actor, shortened to Ron
to do is to act

explanation.surface: Go and watch Ronald Colman performing to music.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronald Colman was a 1930s Hollywood star; 'See' just invites us to watch.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondo is a piece of music in which a principal theme returns between contrasting episodes.

clue.text: Low type of balloon

explanation.surface: A kind of low-flying balloon.
explanation.walkthrough: David Low was a cartoonist whose Colonel Blimp became the type of the pompous reactionary.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonel Blimp was the stock reactionary created by the cartoonist Low, and a blimp is also a non-rigid airship.

clue.text: No old settler once in the island

parts.note: something new is not old
a guinea was a former British gold coin (21 shillings) used to settle bills

explanation.surface: No longtime colonist lived on the island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'settler' suggests a colonist; it is a coin that settles a debt.
explanation.definitionFit: New Guinea is the large island north of Australia.

clue.text: But the parson's has no connexion with lead

definitions.text: But the parson's has no connexion with lead

parts.words: But the parson's has no connexion with lead
parts.note: a pet's neckband has a leash clipped to it, but the clergyman's stiff white band of the same name has none

explanation.walkthrough: 'lead' looks like the metal or leadership; it is a dog's leash.
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman's stiff white collar is nicknamed after the band worn by a pet.

clue.text: Knock back oriental wine — a figure of speech

indicators.note: Knock back says the oriental wine is drunk down and so read backwards

parts.note: E is short for east, oriental
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: Down an eastern wine while using rhetorical language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock back' is to drink, but here reverses EPORT.
explanation.definitionFit: A trope is a figurative use of language, such as metaphor.
